items.title: Atlas Sound Surprise Releases First Album in 15 Years
items.summary:
Bradford Cox released a new Atlas Sound album without warning this week. Thanatos, the first record under the name in 15 years, is streaming now, with a vinyl edition to follow next year through 4AD. Cox paired the release with a scent map listeners can follow along with and a video titled "A Visit With Bradford Cox."

Pitchfork reported that the album closes out a trilogy begun with Logos and Parallax, according to a press release accompanying the record. Cox played every instrument and sang every part himself, then sent the finished tracks to Heba Kadry for mastering. The credits also thank his dog, Faulkner, for emotional support in the studio, and the cover, shot by Javier Morales, shows a sculpture by Chris Reynolds.

The surprise drop caps a busy few months for the Deerhunter frontman, who had kept both of his bands largely quiet since 2019, the year Deerhunter put out Why Hasn't Everything Already Disappeared? Cox returned to the stage at Making Time ∞ festival in September and released "Octoberland" last month, his first single since Parallax.

Cate Le Bon, a longtime collaborator, wrote the album bio. "Virginia Woolf accessed her enormous eye by leaving the house," she wrote. "Bradford Cox finds it by burrowing deeper inside the familiar shell that is his home. Sheltered from all exterior weather fronts. surrounded by objects he has collected and absorbed for decades and held by the warmth of the love of his life. He has consumed it all and transformed geometrical space into a living burial chamber where he can shed the self."

Le Bon described the record as "lyrically led by a disassociated primordial wisdom usually found in the sediment of dreams," and as "the past sung without memory of it but evoked by an action, a gesture, a ritual, a will." For now, Thanatos exists only as a stream; the physical release arrives in 2026.

items.title: Mike D: Tiny Desk Concert
items.summary:
Mike D of the Beastie Boys has played a Tiny Desk concert, performing beats and verses that turn on what NPR Music described as reflections on the vast mysteries of life.

He brought a band with him for the set behind the desk, an outfit NPR characterized as energetic. Among its members are two of his own sons.

items.title: Blondie Are Waiting for the Clouds to Part on Wistful New Song ‘Come Back Home’
items.summary:
Blondie has released "Come Back Home," the second single from High Noon, the band's album due February 26. The song was written by Jess Wolfe and Holly Laessig of Lucius, who also sing harmonies on the recording. Its melody runs bright against lyrics about wanting somewhere to stay put.

Wolfe and Laessig told Rolling Stone the track started as something personal before it reached Blondie. "We had been on tour for a few years, and wrote this song; a sort of reflection of being away for too long, and the ways in which distance and the road can mess with your mind and your relationships," they said in a statement. They added that they grew up with Debbie Harry as "the ultimate female icon of punk, rock, and disco" and never expected a song of theirs to enter the band's catalog.

Guitarist Chris Stein compared the single's mood to Alison Krauss's "Down to the River to Pray" from the Coen brothers' O Brother, Where Art Thou?, pointing to a shared sense of restraint and an almost spiritual quality.

High Noon is Blondie's first album in nine years and their first new music since 2017's Pollinator. The 13-track record was led by "Spectral Eyes," written by Johnny Marr and released in October, and also includes Stein's "Heartbreak Kid," Glen Matlock's "Sleepwalking," and "Man Who Had No Face," which Stein co-wrote with Harry.

The album revisits "Little Metal Drummer," a song originally cut by founding keyboardist Jimmy Destri for his 1981 solo debut Heart On A Wall. Harry and founding drummer Clem Burke, who died in April 2025, both played on that original recording. "This album is classic Blondie — an amalgamation of all our different influences and eras into something new," Harry said in an earlier statement.
